n: The book’s great appeal to the young: remember your Creator now, before the hard years of old age arrive when life feels joyless. Choosing God early shapes everything.

f.g: Troubled years of old age and decline.

n: Before life’s lights grow dim and troubles keep returning like clouds after rain. Many read verses 2–6 as a poetic picture of growing old.

f.w: the clouds return after the rain
f.g: Troubles that keep coming back, one after another.

n: In old age, the “keepers of the house” (hands and arms) shake, the “strong men” (legs) bend, the “grinders” (teeth) are few, and the “windows” (eyes) grow dim.

f.w: those that look out of the windows

n: The “doors” (ears or lips) close, sounds grow faint, the elderly wake at the first birdsong, and singing voices fade.

f.w: rise up at the voice of the bird
f.g: Wake very early, as the elderly often do.
Songs or singing voices — or the voice and hearing.

n: The old fear heights and dangers on the road; hair turns white like almond blossoms; even a grasshopper feels heavy; and desire fades — until one goes to his eternal home amid mourners.

f.g: Almond blossoms are white — a picture of white hair.

n: Before life’s thread snaps: a silver cord breaks, a golden lamp-bowl shatters, the water jar breaks at the spring, the well’s wheel falls apart. All are images of death.

f.g: Often understood as the cord of life that holds the lamp, or the bond between body and spirit.
A lamp bowl hanging from a cord; when it falls, the light goes out.

n: At death the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Latter-day Saints see here the truth that our spirits came from God and return to Him.

f.w: the dust return to the earth
the spirit shall return unto God who gave it

n: The book ends where it began: life lived only “under the sun” is a passing breath. This frame prepares for the final conclusion.
A narrator now describes the Preacher: because he was wise, he kept teaching people, carefully studying and arranging many proverbs.
The Preacher looked for pleasing, fitting words, and what he wrote was honest and true.
Wise sayings are like goads that prod oxen forward and like firmly driven nails that hold steady. They all come from one Shepherd — God.

f.g: Pointed sticks used to prod livestock.

n: Be warned, my son: there is no end to writing books, and endless study wears out the body. Learning is good, but it must lead somewhere.
The conclusion of everything: reverence God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole purpose of human life. Here the book’s search finds its answer.

f.w: Fear God, and keep his commandments

f.g: Literally “this is the whole of man” — what every person is for.

n: God will judge every deed, even secret ones, whether good or evil. Because judgment is real, life is not meaningless after all.
